name: Price and process owner changes
summary: When the consultant proposes a change, an RFI answer adds scope or the site finds a condition the drawings did not show, the project team prices the change and asks the owner to pay for it. The assistant project manager collects subcontractor quotes, an estimator prices self-performed work, the project manager signs the quotation and negotiates it with the consultant and owner, and the owner either issues a change order, directs the work at a price to be agreed, or declines. Most of the elapsed time is waiting: for trade quotes, for the consultant's review and for owner signing authority, while revision cycles and disputed pricing tie up cash for the contractor and its trades.

baseline.org_archetype: A Canadian national general contractor with about 220 active building projects run by project managers and assistant project managers from regional offices.
baseline.notes: Change events are logged in a project management platform, priced in spreadsheets and estimating software, and entered in the construction ERP once executed. Contracts are mostly CCDC 2 (stipulated price) and CCDC 5 (construction management) with owner supplementary conditions.

trigger: The consultant issues a proposed change notice, an RFI answer or site instruction adds scope, the site finds a changed condition, or an owner requests or directs a change.
end_state: An executed change order is entered in the ERP and released to trades, or the event is closed as no change, withdrawn by the owner, or referred to the claims process as a disputed change.

volume.seasonality: Higher from May to November when most building work is in progress; lower in January and February.

evidence.note: Organisation file estimate: about 4 change events per active project a month across 220 projects. Kept unchanged.

surge.cause: Public owners commit remaining capital budgets before their 31 March fiscal year-end, issuing extra scope changes

evidence.note: Author's estimate from the public fiscal year-end spending pattern of hospitals, school boards and universities.
Entitlement, sign-off, negotiation and travel; FTE is the author's estimate (about 18% of 110 project managers). Loaded cost from the organisation file (salaried wage x 1.35).
Logs, scopes, compiles and chases most changes; FTE is the author's estimate (about 21% of 140). Loaded cost from the organisation file (salaried wage x 1.35).
Prices self-performed work on request; FTE is the author's estimate. Loaded cost from the organisation file (salaried wage x 1.35).

Time impact analyses; FTE is the author's estimate. Loaded cost from the organisation file (salaried wage x 1.35).
Approves large quotations and escalations; FTE is the author's estimate. Loaded cost from the organisation file (salaried wage x 1.35).
Enters executed change orders; FTE is the author's estimate. Loaded cost from the organisation file (salaried wage x 1.35).

systems.name: Project management platform (drawings, RFIs, submittals, daily logs, change events)
Take-off and estimating software with Excel bid sheets
Equipment management (fleet register, rates, maintenance work orders)
CPM scheduling software (Primavera P6, Microsoft Project)
Construction ERP (job cost, general ledger, payables, receivables, payroll)
Field time capture (paper sheets or tablet app keyed to cost codes)

resources.name: Telehandlers, skid steers and aerial work platforms

steps.name: Log the change event
steps.description: The assistant project manager opens a new change event in the project platform for a consultant's proposed change notice, an RFI answer that adds scope, a site instruction or an owner request. They give it a number, link the source document, drawings and photos, and tag the likely cost codes.
inputs: proposed change notice, RFI response, site instruction or owner request

error.defect_description: Wrong origin recorded or source documents not linked.

evidence.note: Changes are identified through site instructions, RFIs, submittal comments or other methods; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Decide whether the work is a change
steps.description: The project manager reads the change event against the drawings, specifications, tender clarifications and the prime contract. They decide whether the work is outside the contract scope and worth a quotation, or already included, and note any schedule effect.

error.defect_description: Treats in-scope work as a change, or misses a valid change.

next.condition: already in contract scope; closed as no change

evidence.note: Share of events closed as no change is the author's estimate for a stipulated price and CM portfolio.

steps.name: Give written notice of the change
steps.description: The assistant project manager sends the consultant and owner a notice that the instruction or condition is a change, with a first view of cost and time effects. The notice protects the right to claim later if the price is disputed.

error.defect_description: Notice late or missing the time effect.

control.basis: Prime contract change and claim notice provisions (CCDC 2 Part 6 and GC 6.6)

next.condition: condition must be seen on site with the consultant

evidence.note: CCDC 2 requires findings on claims for a change in Contract Price; share needing a site visit is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Travel to site for a joint review
steps.description: The project manager drives from the regional office to the site and walks the affected area with the superintendent and the consultant's representative. They agree what has changed, take photos and measurements and note whether hidden conditions must be opened up.

next.condition: concealed condition must be opened up

evidence.note: Joint site reviews are booked around the consultant's site visits and owner access windows in occupied buildings; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Open up the concealed condition
steps.description: The superintendent assigns a carpentry and labour crew with a telehandler to open ceilings, walls or excavations so the consultant can see the condition. Before work starts the crew completes a hazard assessment and checks the designated substances report.

control.basis: Ontario OHSA and O. Reg. 213/91: field-level hazard assessment and designated substances report before opening walls or excavating

evidence.note: Crew and telehandler are taken from base-contract work and the step waits until one is free; crew time is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Define the change scope and affected trades
steps.description: The assistant project manager writes a scope sheet with marked-up sketches and quantities, lists the subcontracts and self-performed work affected, and sets up cost codes. The scope sheet becomes the basis for every price request.

error.defect_description: Affected trade or scope item missed.

evidence.note: The contractor prices the contemplated change and obtains subcontractor pricing; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Request trade prices
steps.description: The assistant project manager sends the scope sheet to each affected subcontractor with a request for a priced breakdown and a due date, which starts a subcontract change case for each trade. Self-perform-only changes go straight to the estimator.

error.defect_description: Request sent to the wrong trade or without the latest drawings.

evidence.note: Share of changes with trade work is the author's estimate; most building work is subcontracted.

steps.name: Wait for subcontractor quotes
steps.description: Subcontractors price the change with their own suppliers and sub-trades and return quotes by email. Late or missing quotes are the most common reason a change quotation cannot be assembled.

evidence.note: Missing subcontractor pricing delays proposals for weeks or months (USACE-AGC); range is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Review and level trade quotes
steps.description: The assistant project manager checks each quote against the scope sheet and the subcontract unit rates and markups, and looks for gaps and double counting between trades. Quotes with errors go back to the trade.

error.defect_description: Markup above the subcontract allowance or a scope gap missed.

evidence.note: More than half of change requests need two or more revision cycles (Clearstory survey); shares are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Price self-performed work
steps.description: The estimator does a take-off of the concrete, formwork or carpentry work, applies crew productivity, union labour rates and company equipment rates, and adds materials from current supplier prices. The price goes on the company's own change estimate sheet.

evidence.note: Estimators also carry tender deadlines, so change pricing waits days; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Assess the schedule effect
steps.description: The scheduler inserts the change activities as a fragment into the current CPM schedule update and measures the effect on the critical path and completion date. The result supports any request for more contract time.

evidence.note: A reasonable time analysis is needed to support a time extension request (USACE-AGC); times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Compile the change quotation
steps.description: The assistant project manager builds the quotation summary: trade prices, self-perform cost, general conditions, contract fee and any time request, with each quote attached as backup. They write a short narrative of why the work is a change.

error.defect_description: Arithmetic or markup error, or backup missing.

evidence.note: A quality proposal has a merit narrative and a cost breakdown the reviewer can check (USACE-AGC).

steps.name: Review and sign the quotation
steps.description: The project manager checks the quotation for scope, markups, fee and time, compares it with the project budget and the owner's likely position, and signs it. Errors go back to the assistant project manager; large values need the operations manager.

control.basis: Company delegation of authority: project manager signs change quotations up to a set value

evidence.note: Project managers split time between office and site; shares are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Operations manager approves a large quotation
steps.description: The operations manager reviews large or unusual quotations for margin, risk and the effect on the owner relationship before they go out. They sign or ask for changes.

control.basis: Company delegation of authority for quotations above the project manager limit

evidence.note: Threshold share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Submit the quotation to the consultant
steps.description: The assistant project manager issues the quotation to the consultant and owner through the project platform or email and logs the submission date. The open quotation is listed in the change log reviewed at each owner meeting.

evidence.note: Contractor sends the quote back to the consultant and owner's project manager.

steps.name: Wait for consultant and owner review
steps.description: The consultant and the owner's cost consultant review the quotation in detail against their own estimate, and the owner checks budget and signing authority. They approve, ask questions, issue a change directive or decline.

next.condition: no answer by the follow-up date

evidence.note: Owner review includes a detailed check of the quote and signing authority; the USACE median of 55 days from proposal to modification is slower than this mix of private and public owners.

steps.name: Chase the overdue response
steps.description: The assistant project manager raises the overdue quotation in the weekly owner meeting and by email, and notes the follow-up in the change log. Some owners hold changes until funds are approved.

evidence.note: Owner lack of funds and staff shortfalls slow modifications (USACE-AGC).

steps.name: Read the owner response and route it
steps.description: The project manager reads the response and decides the next move: accept the change order, negotiate a reduced price, proceed under a change directive while price is settled, or close the event if the owner does not proceed.

error.defect_description: Accepts a reduction that leaves trade costs unrecovered.

evidence.note: Owner outcomes (approval, not approved due to cost, change directive) from the Alberta flowcharts; shares are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Negotiate price and time
steps.description: The project manager meets or calls the consultant and owner, goes through the cost breakdown line by line, and trades items until both sides agree or reach an impasse. Agreed changes go to change order; others are revised or escalated.

error.defect_description: Concession not recorded in the trade prices.

evidence.note: Disputed pricing and backup are the main reasons for reduced change payments; shares are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Record time and materials on change directive work
steps.description: The superintendent records daily labour, equipment and material used on the directed work on force-account sheets and gets them signed by the consultant's site representative. Unsigned sheets are the main cause of later disputes.

error.defect_description: Sheets unsigned or equipment hours missing.

evidence.note: Contractor proceeds under a change directive before price is agreed and cannot invoice until a change order is issued.

steps.name: Price the change directive from actual costs
steps.description: The assistant project manager prices the signed force-account sheets, trade invoices and equipment rates into a final quotation. Only costs that contribute directly to the directed work are claimable.

control.basis: CCDC 2-2020 GC 6.3.7 cost rules for valuing a change directive

evidence.note: GC 6.3.7 limits change directive costs to those contributing directly to it.

steps.name: Check the signed change order
steps.description: The assistant project manager compares the change order issued by the consultant with the agreed quotation, checking price, time, scope wording and signatures. A change order that differs goes back to negotiation.

evidence.note: Change order issued under signing authority after approval of the quote; wait for signature routing is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Enter the change order in the ERP
steps.description: The project accountant enters the executed change order in the ERP: contract value, billing schedule line and budget by cost code. Revenue on the change can be billed only after this entry.

control.basis: Contract revenue changes recorded only from executed change orders (IFRS 15 contract modification)

evidence.note: Contractors invoice only against an approved change order; batching to the monthly cost cycle is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Release the approved scope to trades and site
steps.description: The assistant project manager tells the superintendent and affected subcontractors that the change is approved so subcontract change orders can be issued and the work billed. The change log is closed for the event.

evidence.note: Standard project practice; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Prepare a notice of dispute
steps.description: The project manager writes up the disputed change with the quotation, correspondence and the consultant's finding, and drafts a notice of dispute. The notice must go out within the contract's time limit after the finding.

control.basis: CCDC 2 Part 8: notice of dispute within 15 Working Days of the Consultant's finding

evidence.note: Part 8 notice periods from the law firm summary.

steps.name: Decide whether to escalate
steps.description: The operations manager reviews the disputed change and decides whether to refer it to the claims manager, hold it for a global settlement at closeout, or accept the owner's figure. Accepted figures go back to change order.

control.basis: Company delegation of authority for disputes and claims

next.condition: referred to claims or held for global settlement

evidence.note: Shares are the author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Concealed condition opened up
exceptions.description: The change cannot be priced until a crew opens walls, ceilings or an excavation for the consultant to see, which needs a free crew and a hazard assessment.

exceptions.name: Trade quote revision loop
exceptions.description: A subcontractor quote with wrong scope or excess markup goes back for revision, adding another wait for quotes.

exceptions.name: Change directive priced from actual cost
exceptions.description: The owner directs the work before price is agreed; the site records force-account time and the team prices actual costs afterwards.

exceptions.name: Disputed change
exceptions.description: Negotiation fails and the project manager issues a notice of dispute for the claims process.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from change event logged to executed change order or closure
benchmarks.population: Change events on Canadian non-residential building projects, 2019-2022

evidence.note: Author's estimate: shorter than the USACE federal figures (about 30 days to propose plus a 55-day median to modification) because many events here are small, private-owner or closed early; close to the 22 + 26 days the Clearstory survey reports for the trade-level equivalent.

benchmarks.unit: average calendar days from request for proposal to contractor proposal
benchmarks.population: USACE vertical building and public works contracts, contractor change registers

evidence.note: US federal owner; used as an outer reference.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from proposal received to signed modification
benchmarks.population: USACE vertical building and public works contracts

evidence.note: US federal owner, typically slower than Canadian private owners.

benchmarks.population: US specialty contractors (survey with Dodge Construction Network), 2026

evidence.note: Published after the reference period and measured at the trade level.

pain_points.description: Late or incomplete subcontractor quotes hold up the whole quotation.

evidence.note: Missing subcontractor pricing delays proposals for weeks or months.

pain_points.description: Quotations wait weeks for consultant review and owner signing authority, and are chased in owner meetings.

evidence.note: Median 55 days from proposal to modification for USACE.

pain_points.description: Disputed pricing and thin backup trigger revision cycles and reduced settlements.

evidence.note: 66% of GCs cite disputed pricing and 53% insufficient backup.

pain_points.description: Work under a change directive cannot be billed until a change order is issued, so the contractor finances it.

evidence.note: Contractors cannot invoice against a change directive.

sources.title: Construction Contract Modifications: A Joint Study by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and Associated General Contractors of America
sources.publisher: Associated General Contractors of America and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
sources.supports: Contractor change registers overlaid on USACE change logs (vertical building and public works, design-bid-build and design-build): a general contractor submitted a proposal about 30 days after a request for proposal on average; the government issued the modification on average within 90 days of proposal receipt, median 55 days; causes include disagreement on merit, requests for more documentation, missing subcontractor pricing delaying proposals for weeks or months, and change volume exceeding staff; contractors log a change when notified by RFI response or submittal comment, on average 30 days before the government records it.

sources.title: 2026 State of Change Orders: Specialty Contractor Report
sources.supports: Survey of US general and specialty contractors: average 22 days from a signed T&M tag to a fully priced change order request; average 26 days from change order request submission to a signed change order from the GC; 43% wait three weeks or more; 97% sometimes start work before approval, 42% more than half the time; more than half of requests need two or more revision cycles; GCs cite disputed pricing (66%) and insufficient backup (53%) when reducing payment; 48% have had disputes escalate to arbitration or legal process.

sources.title: Change Process for Construction Management Contracts (flowchart CA_MC_605_TRC)
sources.supports: Public owner change process: project team identifies a potential change through site instructions, RFIs or other methods; consultant prepares a change request with cost estimate and reasons, signed under expenditure signing authority; consultant issues a contemplated change notice for pricing; the construction manager prices it, obtaining subcontractor pricing; consultant and cost consultant review the quote in detail; if not agreed the change is not approved due to cost; otherwise a change authorization or change order is issued and the contractor proceeds.

sources.title: Change Directive (CD) Process (flowchart CA_MC_660_TRC)
sources.supports: For urgent changes the consultant prepares a change directive with a maximum upset price, signed under expenditure signing authority, directing the contractor to proceed before price is agreed; a final quotation is then requested and a change order issued; contractors cannot invoice against a change directive, only against an approved change order.

sources.title: Practice Tip PT.23.11: CCDC 2-2020 Stipulated Price Contract, Overview of the Changes in the 2020 Version and Recommended Supplementary Conditions
sources.supports: CCDC 2-2020 GC 6.3.7: change directive costs apply in as much as they contribute directly to implementing the change directive; GC 8.2 adjudication added to align with the Construction Act; negotiation-mediation-arbitration dispute procedure; Consultant must make findings on claims for a change in Contract Price regardless of size or number (GC 2.2.11); GC 6.6.5 allows more time for findings on detailed claims.

sources.title: The new CCDC 2 - 2020: contract changes you need to know
sources.supports: CCDC 2-2020 revises the list of claimable actual costs for change directives to those contributing directly to the change directive (GC 6.3.7); contract does not affect rights to statutory adjudication; GC 6.5.2 delay by stop work order extends contract time with reasonable delay costs.

sources.title: Construction Industry Disputes: Use Of Negotiation, Mediation And Arbitration Clause
sources.publisher: Goldman Sloan Nash & Haber LLP (via Legal 500 / Mondaq)
sources.supports: CCDC Part 8: a party may refer a dispute to the Consultant for a written finding; notice of dispute within 15 Working Days of the finding, reply within 10 Working Days; amicable negotiation; Project Mediator appointed within 20 Working Days of award; mediation non-binding; if mediation fails either party may refer the dispute to arbitration within 10 Working Days; litigation remains if the parties do not agree to arbitrate.

assumptions: Unit of work is one change event as logged by the project team, including events later closed as no change or withdrawn; this keeps the volume consistent with the organisation file (about 900 a month).
The trade pricing inside s07 to s09 is the subcontract change process seen from the owner change; trade-side steps are in gc-ops-subtrade-change.
Project manager travel uses the manager's own vehicle with a mileage allowance, so no company vehicle resource is tied up.
Construction of the change work itself belongs to site coordination and self-perform processes; only opening up concealed conditions for pricing is modelled here.
Loops for chasing the owner restart the full owner-review wait, which slightly overstates long tails.
Contract notice and cost rules are modelled as policy controls because they come from contracts, not statute.
Waits include nights and weekends; project office roles work weekdays.

Simulated hands-on time (mean about 10.5 hours per event, including revision and chase loops) implies about 73 FTE against 64.5 stated; the stated figures assume part of the assistant project manager and project manager time is absorbed in owner meetings counted under other processes.
